paragraphs: The paper develops a hierarchical Bayesian model for representing structure in natural images. Its starting point is independent component analysis, which describes an image through coefficients associated with an image basis. The proposed model extends this approach nonlinearly to capture relationships that an independence assumption would leave out.

The key change concerns the joint distribution of those coefficients. Instead of treating them as independent, the model adapts their distribution to the way their variances are structured. This shifts attention toward patterns in how strongly different coefficients vary, providing a description of higher-order image structure beyond the individual coefficients themselves.

The resulting representation offers a way to learn abstract properties such as object location, scale, and texture. These properties are represented through sparse, distributed activity with coarse coding: the representation spreads information across components rather than assigning every property to a single exact indicator. The contribution is a modeling framework connecting variance structure to more abstract image descriptions.
neurips-2002-a-model-for-learning-varian.tldr: A hierarchical Bayesian extension of independent component analysis models image-coefficient variance structure to learn sparse representations of abstract image properties.

paragraphs: Two sequences can describe the same event without progressing in exact synchrony. This paper develops a hidden Markov model architecture for representing the joint probability of such paired sequences. Audio-visual speech recognition provides its application: the model must account for the relationship between the two streams while allowing their alignment to vary.

The architecture draws on asynchronous input/output hidden Markov models and pair hidden Markov models. The authors provide an expectation-maximization algorithm for learning its parameters, together with a Viterbi decoder. The decoder finds both an optimal hidden-state sequence and an alignment between the observed sequences, making synchronization part of the inference problem.

Tests on the M2VTS audio-visual speech database yielded robust performance across various noise conditions. This supports the usefulness of the architecture for the tested recognition task. Its methodological contribution is to bring paired observations, asynchronous alignment, model training, and decoding into a single probabilistic framework for sequences describing a shared event.
neurips-2002-an-asynchronous-hidden-mark.tldr: An asynchronous hidden Markov model jointly learns and aligns paired sequences, showing robust audio-visual speech recognition under varied noise conditions.

paragraphs: Neurons can respond very differently to the same sensory input, raising the question of how to group them by function. The paper formalizes a useful intuition: a good classification should explain much of this response diversity through the group a neuron belongs to, while leaving less diversity among neurons within each group.

The authors express this objective using information theory. Their approach does not require a predefined distance measure between stimuli or between responses. This matters because deciding what counts as a similar response can otherwise become a separate modeling choice that shapes the resulting groups before classification even begins.

Applied to salamander retinal ganglion cells, the method recovers established classifications and supplies clear evidence for additional subclasses. Yet group membership does not erase individual differences: the authors find that every recorded ganglion cell is functionally distinctive, with only a few spikes needed to distinguish cells reliably even within a subclass. The results support both useful categories and meaningful individuality.
neurips-2002-an-information-theoretic-ap.tldr: Information-theoretic clustering identifies established and additional retinal neuron subclasses while revealing distinctive responses within each subclass.

paragraphs: This paper investigates a Bayesian approach to estimating integrals from sampled function values. The central idea is to incorporate prior knowledge about the function being integrated, such as its smoothness. That information can influence the estimate, allowing relationships between sampled values to contribute to the calculation.

For one simple problem, the authors show that Bayesian Monte Carlo outperforms any classical importance sampling method. They also investigate harder multidimensional integrals used to compute statistical model evidence, also called marginal likelihoods or partition functions. In those investigations, Bayesian Monte Carlo outperformed Annealed Importance Sampling; these findings concern the problems studied rather than every possible integration task.

The authors identify very high dimensionality and extensive multimodality as settings where the method may be less suitable. They also highlight flexibility in choosing sample distributions. Because samples can come from any distribution, there is a possibility of actively selecting evaluation points to maximize information gain, turning sample placement into part of the estimation strategy.
neurips-2002-bayesian-monte-carlo-840ccc.tldr: Bayesian Monte Carlo uses prior knowledge about integrands to improve integration in studied problems and enables potentially informative sample selection.

paragraphs: The paper examines how individual neurons in rat auditory cortex respond to brief tones. Using cell-attached recordings to isolate single neurons, the researchers found that most showed approximately binary responses: a tone usually elicited either no spike or one spike, with few responses containing multiple spikes.

Some especially striking neurons produced exactly one spike on every trial, showing no variation in spike count across repeated presentations. Many neurons were also selective for tone frequency. Because most individual responses contained at most one spike, the authors locate frequency information in the population response, information that would not be available to later processing restricted to a single unit.

The authors argue that these binary units permit a more efficient population code than conventional rate-coding units. They also interpret the observations as consistent with a model in which synchronized packets of spikes travel stably between neuronal populations. That compatibility provides a possible processing interpretation; the recordings themselves establish the reported response pattern under the studied tone conditions.
neurips-2002-binary-coding-in-auditory-c.tldr: Single-neuron recordings reveal largely zero-or-one-spike responses to brief tones, supporting a population-based account of auditory frequency coding.

paragraphs: Similarity data describe how alike objects are, but a representation must explain what underlies those relationships. This paper introduces a model that combines continuous dimensions with discrete features. It therefore provides room for both graded differences between objects and distinctions expressed through separate features within the same learned representation.

The contribution includes an algorithm for learning these mixed representations from similarity data. The authors also develop a Bayesian model selection approach to choose how many dimensions and features to include. Learning the representation and selecting its size address different questions: what structure explains the similarities, and how much representational structure should be used.

The approach is demonstrated on a classic dataset of similarities among the numbers zero through nine. This supplies a concrete setting for showing how continuous and discrete components can be considered together. The paper's stated contribution is the combined model, its learning procedure, and its model selection method, illustrated through that similarity dataset.
neurips-2002-combining-dimensions-and-fe.tldr: A similarity model combines continuous dimensions and discrete features, with Bayesian selection of how many of each to use.

paragraphs: Fitting a mixture model involves searching a likelihood surface whose shape can affect how learning proceeds. This paper shows that critical points in mixture-type models can form entire lines. These lines arise by embedding a critical point from a model with fewer components into a model with more components.

The result connects the optimization geometry of models of different sizes. A solution in the smaller model can correspond to a family of critical configurations in the larger one. The authors also derive a sufficient condition for identifying when such a critical line consists of local maxima or saddle points. A sufficient condition establishes a case where the conclusion holds without claiming to cover every case.

Using this analysis, the paper proposes a component-splitting method for Gaussian mixture models. The method turns the structural result about critical lines into a practical approach to modifying mixture components. Experiments verify its effectiveness, connecting the theoretical account of the likelihood surface with an evaluated learning procedure.
neurips-2002-critical-lines-in-symmetry-.tldr: An analysis of critical lines in mixture-model likelihoods motivates a Gaussian component-splitting method whose effectiveness is verified experimentally.

paragraphs: Activity in the striatum of awake monkeys depends strongly on the reward expected from a behavior. This paper uses a computational model of spiny neurons, the striatum's principal neurons, to investigate a possible mechanism. The hypothesis is that dopamine directly alters their activity through activation of D1 receptors.

In the model, dopamine strengthens key ionic currents and produces bistability, meaning that the system can support two stable states. This changes more than the maximum firing rate. It also makes the response depend on timing and on the neuron's state, adding a dynamic component to how inputs are processed.

These modeled changes improve the detectability of inputs that are correlated over time. The result offers a mechanistic account of how dopamine could influence which temporal signals become noticeable in neuronal activity. Because the work assesses a hypothesis computationally, its contribution is support for this proposed mechanism within the model, rather than direct confirmation that it explains all reward-dependent activity.
neurips-2002-dopamine-induced-bistabilit.tldr: A spiny-neuron model links dopamine-induced bistability to stronger detection of temporally correlated inputs.

paragraphs: The paper studies how well certain learning methods in Hilbert function spaces generalize beyond their training data. These spaces provide the setting for the kernel learning problems considered. The authors introduce a scale-sensitive effective data dimension to describe the complexity relevant to learning, rather than relying only on the formal dimension of the surrounding space.

They show that this effective dimension characterizes the convergence rate of the underlying learning problem. In practical terms, the concept connects the relevant complexity of the data with how quickly learning improves as information accumulates. Its scale sensitivity means that complexity is considered at the level relevant to the analysis, rather than treated as one fixed dimension.

This framework extends results from finite-dimensional parametric estimation to nonparametric kernel methods. The authors derive upper bounds on generalization performance and show that the resulting convergence rates are optimal under various circumstances. The optimality claim is conditional on those circumstances, while the broader contribution is a shared language for analyzing these different learning settings.
neurips-2002-effective-dimension-and-gen.tldr: Scale-sensitive effective dimension characterizes convergence in kernel learning and yields generalization bounds with optimal rates under various conditions.

paragraphs: Understanding a sensory neuron requires estimating how a changing stimulus produces its response. The paper considers experiments that present rapidly varying, complex inputs while recording neuronal activity. The estimation problem is to recover a stimulus-response function that explains the observed firing and can predict responses to new inputs.

The authors connect commonly used correlation-based techniques, including Wiener filtering and Wiener or Volterra kernel estimation, to maximum likelihood regression with Gaussian output noise. They then explore Bayesian evidence optimization as a way to condition these estimates. This introduces learned controls over the structure of the estimated transformation.

Specifically, the method learns hyperparameters governing smoothness and sparsity. These determine how smoothly the estimated function varies and how concentrated its representation is. The authors show that learning these controls can dramatically improve estimate quality, judged by prediction on novel stimuli. The finding matters because the benefit is assessed through responses beyond the inputs used to construct the estimate.
neurips-2002-evidence-optimization-techn.tldr: Bayesian evidence optimization learns smoothness and sparsity controls that can dramatically improve neural response predictions for novel stimuli.

paragraphs: The paper introduces forward decoding kernel machines for estimating sequences, with continuous phone recognition as the application. The method combines large-margin classifiers with hidden Markov models. It performs adaptive maximum a posteriori sequence estimation, bringing a kernel-based probability model into the process of deciding how hidden states change over time.

A central feature is that state transitions depend on the observed data. The probability model is trained recursively using a scheme designed to handle noisy and partially labeled observations. For large training sets, the authors use a sparse probabilistic support vector machine based on quadratic entropy, together with an online stochastic steepest descent algorithm.

In speaker-independent continuous phone recognition, the system was trained on 177,080 TIMIT samples and achieved 80.6% recognition accuracy across the full test set. This result was obtained without a prior phonetic language model. The finding demonstrates the combined sequence and kernel approach in the stated recognition setting, while the training design addresses the practical demands of large, imperfectly labeled datasets.
neurips-2002-forward-decoding-kernel-bas.tldr: Forward decoding kernel machines combine kernel classifiers and hidden Markov models, achieving 80.6% TIMIT phone recognition accuracy without a prior phonetic language model.

paragraphs: This paper approaches clustering through the behavior of a Markov chain on a dataset. Probability mass moves between data points according to transition probabilities. The goal is to identify stable groups and automatically determine their number by examining how that probability flow behaves as the chain is repeatedly updated.

The authors derive eigenflows from the spectral properties of the transition matrix. Each eigenflow describes a component of probability movement, with an eigenvalue determining how quickly it decays. Its half-life expresses that decay in temporal terms. An ideal stable cluster has no eigenflow leaving it and an infinite half-life.

The key step is to examine how an eigenflow's half-life changes when edge weights change. This sensitivity identifies bottlenecks connecting otherwise weakly coupled clusters. The proposed EIGENCUTS algorithm repeatedly removes those bottlenecks to form clusters. The approach turns the stability of probability flow into a criterion for deciding where to separate the data, rather than requiring a cluster count in advance.
neurips-2002-half-lives-of-eigenflows-fo.tldr: EIGENCUTS identifies stable clusters by measuring how probability-flow half-lives respond to changes in graph connections.

paragraphs: Learning control policies from scratch can be difficult in high-dimensional spaces with continuous states and actions. This paper instead starts from a simple existing policy and learns how to transform it into a more complex movement. The starting policy is represented by differential equations with well-defined attractor and stability properties.

Nonparametric regression supplies a nonlinear transformation of these canonical dynamics. The authors describe how this can generate almost arbitrary nonlinear policies while retaining the original system's stability properties. This makes the starting dynamics a useful foundation: the learned transformation changes the movement while preserving the stated stability behavior.

The method learns movement skills for a humanoid robot from human demonstrations. Policies are acquired rapidly and can be reused or modified online as the environment changes. The regression model's linear parameterization also supports recognizing and classifying previously learned movements. Evaluations in simulation and on a physical humanoid robot with 30 degrees of freedom demonstrate the approach's feasibility and robustness.
neurips-2002-learning-attractor-landscap.tldr: Transforming stable canonical dynamics lets a humanoid robot learn flexible movement skills from demonstrations while retaining stability properties.

paragraphs: Many learning methods depend on a definition of similarity between objects. This paper addresses density estimation when the data may concentrate near a curved, lower-dimensional structure, or manifold. Rather than keeping similarity fixed, the proposed method adapts to local structure so that the density estimate reflects how nearby observations are organized.

The method uses the leading eigenvectors of regularized local covariance matrices. These identify prominent directions of variation around different parts of the data. Incorporating those directions into a nonparametric kernel density estimator gives the model a way to follow local manifold structure, instead of treating every neighborhood according to the same fixed geometry.

Density-estimation experiments show significant improvements over Parzen estimators. The authors also use the estimated densities inside Bayes classifiers, obtaining classification rates similar to support vector machines and substantially better than the Parzen classifier. These reported results connect the learned local geometry to benefits in both density modeling and the classification experiments considered.
neurips-2002-manifold-parzen-windows-29b.tldr: Manifold Parzen windows adapt density estimation to local data geometry, improving on Parzen methods in the reported density and classification experiments.

paragraphs: An information filter must decide which arriving items are relevant, but its decisions can also determine what feedback it receives. This paper studies a setting where an item's label becomes visible only when the filter marks it relevant. Relevance labels are assumed to arise from an unknown probabilistic linear function of the feature vectors.

Starting with an analysis of a restricted version of this model, the authors derive a more general filtering rule based on the margin of a ridge regression estimator. The margin informs the relevance decision, linking prediction to selective feedback. In a real document-filtering experiment, the rule performs close to an online classifier that can observe every label.

The theoretical analysis concerns a randomized variant of the rule. Its expected mistake count is shown to stay within a controlled excess over that of an optimal filter that knows the hidden linear model. The empirical comparison and theoretical guarantee therefore address distinct versions or aspects of the approach, both under the stated information-filtering setup.
neurips-2002-margin-based-algorithms-for.tldr: A ridge-regression margin rule learns with selectively revealed labels, with encouraging document-filtering results and a mistake guarantee for a randomized variant.

paragraphs: The paper introduces NashProp, an algorithm for computing Nash equilibria in multiplayer games represented by undirected graphs. Such a representation organizes the game around relationships between players. NashProp works through repeated local message passing, allowing information relevant to equilibrium computation to move through the graph over successive iterations.

The algorithm generalizes an earlier approach for tree-structured games to arbitrary undirected graphs, including graphs with many loops. The authors describe it as similar in spirit to belief propagation in probabilistic inference. This connection helps explain its design: local exchanges support a computation concerning the whole network of interacting players.

Formal analysis and experiments support its performance on large graphical games containing many loops. In the reported experiments, it often converges in roughly a dozen iterations on graphs with hundreds of nodes. This is an empirical observation rather than a universal convergence promise. The paper positions NashProp alongside junction-tree approaches as another promising general-purpose route to equilibrium computation in graphical games.
neurips-2002-nash-propagation-for-loopy-.tldr: NashProp uses local message passing to compute equilibria in graphical games, often converging quickly on large, loopy graphs in experiments.

paragraphs: This paper presents analog neuromorphic circuits that implement synapses with two linked behaviors: sensitivity to spike timing and a tendency toward two stable long-term strengths. The aim is to realize these learning dynamics directly in electronic hardware. The synapses connect integrate-and-fire neurons in a fabricated prototype VLSI chip.

On short time scales, a synapse's strength changes according to the relative timing of spikes from the neurons before and after it. This is spike-timing-dependent plasticity. Over longer time scales, the strength approaches either a potentiated state or a depressed state, corresponding to the two stable outcomes of the bistable design.

Tests on the chip demonstrate both the timing-dependent learning behavior and the long-term bistable characteristics. The contribution therefore includes physical implementation and experimental verification of the two time scales of synaptic behavior. It shows that a hardware network can combine ongoing timing-sensitive changes with a longer-term tendency toward strengthened or weakened connection states.
neurips-2002-neuromorphic-bisable-vlsi-s.tldr: A prototype neuromorphic chip demonstrates synapses that learn from spike timing and approach one of two stable long-term strengths.

paragraphs: Policy evaluation asks how valuable states are under a particular policy. When the value function is represented with a linear function approximator, reinforcement learning algorithms produce approximate solutions. This paper examines several such solutions and asks what makes each one optimal, given that the representation restricts which value functions can be expressed.

The authors show that each solution optimizes a particular objective function. Consequently, different algorithms can reach different answers while each is optimal according to its own criterion. They also characterize these answers as different projections of the exact value function into the space available to the linear approximator.

The projection view gives a common geometric interpretation of the algorithms. Each operation maps the exact answer into the restricted representation in a different way. The results provide a basis for comparing the error achieved by an algorithm with the error of an optimal approximate solution. They establish objective-specific optimality, rather than identifying a single approximation that is best under every criterion.
neurips-2002-optimality-of-reinforcement.tldr: Several linear policy-evaluation algorithms are shown to optimize distinct objectives and correspond to different projections of the exact value function.

paragraphs: The paper presents a physical implementation of a spiking neuron model based on the FitzHugh-Nagumo equations. It combines optical and electronic components to reproduce important features of the model's dynamics. The contribution concerns how a mathematical neuron model can be realized in a system that accepts real input signals.

A tunable semiconductor laser and a spectral filter create a nonlinear relationship between the driving voltage and the detected signal. Linear electronic feedback completes the implementation. These parts have complementary roles: the optical arrangement supplies the nonlinear mapping, while the feedback connects the output back into the system's continuing dynamics.

The implementation can receive either electronic or optical inputs. Experiments on a single physical system, together with numerical results for interactions between models, confirm that the approach can implement important characteristics of spiking neural models. The evidence thus combines a hardware demonstration of an individual unit with simulated interaction results, supporting the proposed optoelectronic implementation strategy.
neurips-2002-optoelectronic-implementati.tldr: A laser, spectral filter, and electronic feedback implement important features of a FitzHugh-Nagumo spiking neuron model.

paragraphs: A document can belong to several categories at once, making text categorization a problem of assigning multiple labels. This paper proposes probabilistic generative models called parametric mixture models for that setting. The models are designed to detect several categories for the same text within a shared modeling approach.

The conventional approach described in the paper uses a separate binary classifier for each category. Each classifier decides whether its particular label applies. Parametric mixture models instead support simultaneous detection of multiple categories. The authors derive efficient algorithms for both learning the models and using them to predict categories for text.

Experiments use real World Wide Web pages with multiple labels. The authors report that their method could significantly outperform the conventional binary approaches in this setting. This provides empirical support for jointly modeling the categorization problem, while keeping the claim tied to the evaluated text data. The contribution includes both the generative formulation and the algorithms needed to apply it.
neurips-2002-parametric-mixture-models-f.tldr: Parametric mixture models jointly detect multiple text categories and can significantly outperform separate binary classifiers on the evaluated web pages.

paragraphs: Particle filters estimate a changing system's state from sensor observations. In real-time applications, sensors can deliver information faster than the filter can update. A common response is to process observations whenever possible and discard the rest. This paper develops a way to use all arriving sensor information despite that mismatch in rates.

The method represents the posterior distribution as a mixture of sample sets. Each mixture component incorporates one observation received during a filter update. The components' weights are chosen to minimize the approximation error caused by this mixture representation, connecting the use of incoming measurements to the quality of the resulting state estimate.

Through this weighting, computational samples are focused on sensor information that is valuable to the estimate. Experiments with data collected by a mobile robot show strong improvements over the other approaches considered. The result demonstrates that accommodating observations within the representation can improve filtering when computation cannot keep pace with the sensor stream.
neurips-2002-real-time-particle-filters-.tldr: Real-time particle filters use mixtures of sample sets to incorporate all sensor observations even when sensors outpace filter updates.

paragraphs: This paper studies how the learning rate in Population-based Incremental Learning must change as a problem becomes larger. It shows that the required adjustment can be highly sensitive to the problem itself. A learning rate that behaves suitably at one system size therefore cannot simply be carried over without considering this scaling.

The analysis examines two contrasting problems. For a needle-in-a-haystack problem, the learning rate must shrink exponentially with system size. For the smooth-function example, the required decay follows a square-root scaling. These cases establish that the tuning requirement depends strongly on the structure of the optimization problem.

The authors propose two ways to remove this sensitivity. Learning dynamics that obey detailed balance give consistent performance across the full range of learning rates. A mutation-like mechanism still requires the learning rate to decrease inversely with system size, but makes that scaling independent of the problem. The two approaches thus offer different ways to make learning-rate selection more predictable.
neurips-2002-scaling-of-probability-base.tldr: Population-based Incremental Learning needs problem-dependent learning-rate scaling, while detailed-balance dynamics and a mutation-like mechanism offer ways to reduce that sensitivity.

paragraphs: Recovering a scene from an image can require a complex representation of shape or surface properties. This paper proposes a compact alternative called a scene recipe. The representation refers back to the observed image, using information already present there to describe scene detail through a smaller collection of parameters.

Shape recipes implement this idea as regression coefficients that predict bandpassed shape from image data. Rather than storing all shape detail directly in the representation, the coefficients specify a relationship between the image and the shape components being estimated. This makes the image itself part of how the scene is represented.

The authors demonstrate two uses. First, they improve stereo shape estimates by learning recipes at low resolution and applying them at full resolution. Second, they use the lighting and material information implicitly contained in shape recipes for material segmentation. These applications illustrate how a compact image-referencing representation can support both shape estimation and distinctions between materials.
neurips-2002-shape-recipes-scene-represe.tldr: Shape recipes compactly describe shape through image-based regression coefficients and support improved stereo estimates and material segmentation.

paragraphs: Source separation aims to recover individual sources from recordings that contain mixtures of them. This paper develops separation algorithms for sensor arrays using probabilistic graphical models with latent variables. The models explicitly represent hidden structure associated with the sources, providing a framework for explaining how the observed recordings arise.

A central feature is the use of detailed models of source properties. The algorithms also use subband filtering to represent the reverberant environment and explicitly account for background noise and sensor noise. These ingredients distinguish source characteristics, environmental effects, and noise within the overall probabilistic description of the recordings.

The authors use variational techniques to make inference computationally manageable. Specifically, the computation required for each expectation-maximization iteration grows linearly with the number of frames. This is a statement about per-iteration scaling in recording length. The contribution combines richer modeling of the separation problem with an inference approach that preserves that favorable dependence on the amount of recorded data.
neurips-2002-source-separation-with-a-se.tldr: Latent-variable source-separation models combine source detail, reverberation, and noise modeling with computation that scales linearly in frames per EM iteration.

paragraphs: The paper describes the RA scanner, a prototype system for examining finger joints in people with rheumatoid arthritis. Its laser-based imaging technique responds to the optical characteristics of joint tissue. The task is to classify whether a joint's inflammatory status has improved or worsened using the resulting images.

The authors implement and compare several linear and kernel-based classification systems. Because the available dataset is very small, they place particular emphasis on reliable parameter tuning and evaluation. This makes the assessment procedure an important part of the work: the classification models must be evaluated carefully with the limited observations available.

Based on the reported results, the authors conclude that the scanner permits reliable classification of pathological finger joints. They interpret this as support for further development from a prototype toward a product. The evidence concerns the examined system and dataset, and the stated development goal remains a next stage rather than a claim that a finished clinical product was already established.
neurips-2002-the-ra-scanner-prediction-o.tldr: A laser-imaging prototype classifies changes in finger-joint inflammation, with small-dataset results supporting further product development.
